title: Paris with children: the zoo, the aquarium or the Grande Galerie de l'Évolution, and what works on a wet afternoon
subtitle: Four places with animals, living or stuffed, two of them under a roof. Which fits which age, how long each takes, and what the tickets cover.
excerpt: The zoo in the Bois de Vincennes, the old menagerie and the Grande Galerie de l'Évolution in the Jardin des Plantes, and the aquarium at the Trocadéro: what each one is, which suits which age, which are indoors, and what each ticket includes.

meta_title: Paris with kids: zoo, aquarium or Grande Galerie
meta_description: The Vincennes zoo, the Jardin des Plantes and the Aquarium de Paris: which suits which age, which are indoors, and what each ticket includes.

featured_image.alt: A group of giraffes behind a wooden fence among trees at the Paris zoo in the Bois de Vincennes

content_html:
[place attraction="paris-zoological-park" city="paris"]

In the spring of 1827 a giraffe walked from Marseille to Paris. She was a present from Muhammad Ali, the ruler of Egypt, to King Charles X, and no living giraffe had been seen in France before. The last stretch, close to nine hundred kilometres, she did on foot in about six weeks, in an oilskin coat made to her measure, behind the cows whose milk she drank.

She lived for eighteen years in the menagerie of the Jardin des Plantes, and for a season Paris wore giraffe patterns and giraffe-high hair. Children still ask for the giraffes first, and the city has four good answers: a zoo with a whole herd of them, the old menagerie where she lived, a hall where stuffed animals march under a glass roof, and an aquarium dug under a garden. Which one to choose depends on the age of the children and on the sky.

The four at a glance

  • Paris Zoological Park, in the Bois de Vincennes: outdoors, half a day, every age.
  • The menagerie of the Jardin des Plantes: outdoors, small, an hour and a half, best for small children.
  • The Grande Galerie de l'Évolution, in the same garden: indoors, two hours, from about five years old.
  • The Aquarium de Paris, at the Trocadéro: indoors, an hour and a half to two hours, from toddlers up.

The zoo at Vincennes

The zoo opened in 1934, after a temporary one at the Colonial Exhibition of 1931 had drawn crowds. Its landmark is the Grand Rocher, an artificial rock of concrete 65 metres high. It closed in 2008, worn out, and reopened in 2014 rebuilt from the ground: instead of rows of cages there are five landscapes, which the zoo calls biozones (Patagonia, the plains of Sudan and the Sahel, Europe, the Amazon and Guiana, Madagascar).

You walk from sea lions and penguins to giraffes, lions and rhinoceroses, then to wolves and lynxes, and into a very large tropical greenhouse where birds fly loose. There are no elephants and no bears: the new zoo chose fewer species and gave them more room. The enclosures are wide, so an animal can be far away or asleep behind a rock, and small children need lifting and patience.

Allow three to four hours. The nearest metro station is Porte Dorée, about ten minutes on foot. The greenhouse apart, this is an outdoor visit: keep it for a dry day.

The Grand Rocher of 1934 above one of the open enclosures of the rebuilt zoo. Photo: Guilhem Vellut, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The Jardin des Plantes: three visits in one garden

The garden itself is free. Inside it are several buildings of the national natural history museum, and each sells its own ticket.

The menagerie was founded in the 1790s, during the Revolution, with animals from the royal menagerie at Versailles and from street showmen. It is one of the oldest zoos in the world still open. It is small and shady and keeps animals of modest size: red pandas, snow leopards, orang-utans, birds and reptiles. A four-year-old can see everything without being carried.

The Grande Galerie de l'Évolution opened in 1889, was shut in the 1960s for nearly thirty years, and reopened in 1994. In the middle of the hall a procession of African animals crosses the floor: elephants, giraffes, zebras, antelopes, all stuffed, all walking the same way. Above them the light of the glass roof changes through the day, and now and then a storm passes over. A separate children's gallery, for ages six to twelve, has its own timed ticket.

The Gallery of Palaeontology and Comparative Anatomy, five minutes away, is the one for children who love dinosaurs: hundreds of skeletons facing the door on the ground floor, and fossils upstairs. The Gallery of Geology and Mineralogy shows giant crystals.

The Grande Galerie de l'Évolution of 1889, at the end of the Jardin des Plantes. Photo: Alvesgaspar, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The hall of skeletons in the Gallery of Palaeontology and Comparative Anatomy, opened in 1898. Photo: Fulguroblastor, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The Aquarium de Paris

The aquarium lies underground in the gardens of the Trocadéro, across the river from the Eiffel Tower. An aquarium was first dug here for one of the world's fairs of the nineteenth century. It closed in 1985 and reopened, rebuilt, in 2006. The main sights are a large shark tank, the jellyfish, and a pool where children may put a hand in the water and touch the fish.

It is weatherproof and easy with a pushchair, and it fits well with a look at the tower from the Trocadéro terrace. On wet Wednesdays, when many French children have no school, and at weekends it fills up.

What works on a wet afternoon

  • The Grande Galerie and the palaeontology gallery, one after the other. Between them you are outside for five minutes.
  • The aquarium.
  • The Paradox Museum, near the Opéra: rooms of optical illusions made to be photographed. About an hour, best from eight years old to teenagers.
  • The Cité des Sciences at La Villette, with play and discovery areas for children in timed sessions.

Not for rain: the zoo, the menagerie, and Parrot World, an outdoor animal park of South American species east of Paris, near Disneyland, which is hard to reach without a car.

Red pandas in the menagerie of the Jardin des Plantes. Photo: FreCha, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What each ticket includes

  • The zoo entrance ticket covers the five zones and the keepers' presentations. Large bags and suitcases are refused at the gate.
  • The aquarium entrance ticket is for a time slot, and the listing says latecomers are not admitted. It covers entry and the feeding sessions. The listing mentions shows in one place and not in another, so read it.
  • The city walk "with the Grande Galerie ticket" is entry to the Grande Galerie plus an audio walk through central Paris on your phone. There is no commentary inside the museum, and the children's gallery is not included. After buying, you still have to reserve a free time slot on the museum's own website: do it the same day.
  • The Geology and Mineralogy Gallery ticket is entry only, with the same rule about reserving a slot.
  • The Paradox Museum ticket is priority entrance to the exhibits.
  • The Parrot World day ticket is entry to the park outside Paris.

These are the tickets our partner sells for these places, with today's prices:

[partner city="paris" match="galerie,zoological,aquarium,parrot,mineralogy,paradox" limit="6"]

Which one, by age

  • Under five: the aquarium, or the menagerie on a dry day.
  • Five to ten: the Grande Galerie in any weather, the zoo in the sun.
  • Ten and over: the palaeontology gallery, then the Paradox Museum.

Opening days differ from one building to the next, and several of them close one day a week. Current hours are on our pages for the Grande Galerie and the aquarium.

From here

From the Jardin des Plantes it is a short walk to the Arènes de Lutèce, a Roman arena that is now a free public square where children run on the sand. See what else there is in Paris, or open the trip planner for France.

Cover photo: Clem, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0.

faqs.q: What can you do in Paris with children when it rains?
faqs.a: The Grande Galerie de l'Évolution and the palaeontology gallery in the Jardin des Plantes, the Aquarium de Paris at the Trocadéro, and the Paradox Museum near the Opéra are all indoors.

faqs.q: Is the Paris zoo worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, on a dry day and with three to four hours to spare. It was rebuilt between 2008 and 2014 as five landscapes with large enclosures, and it has giraffes, lions, rhinoceroses, penguins and a tropical greenhouse.

faqs.q: How long does the Grande Galerie de l'Évolution take?
faqs.a: About two hours. The children's gallery inside it is a separate timed visit for ages six to twelve.

faqs.q: Is the Aquarium de Paris good for toddlers?
faqs.a: Yes. It is indoors, on a small scale, easy with a pushchair, and has a pool where children can touch the fish. Allow an hour and a half to two hours.

faqs.q: Which is better, the zoo at Vincennes or the menagerie of the Jardin des Plantes?
faqs.a: The zoo is much larger and has the big African animals, and it takes half a day. The menagerie is small, central and suits young children, with red pandas, snow leopards and orang-utans.

title: Day trips from Paris by train beyond Versailles: Chantilly, Rambouillet or the Château de Vincennes
subtitle: Three châteaux with a fraction of the crowds: one for paintings and gardens, one for a quiet park, one at the end of a metro line.
excerpt: Chantilly is 25 minutes from the Gare du Nord, Rambouillet about 35 from Montparnasse, and the Château de Vincennes is at the last stop of metro line 1. What each one offers, how long it takes, which to choose, and what each ticket includes.
focus_keyword: day trips from Paris by train other than Versailles
longtail_phrases: which château near Paris is easiest to reach
is Chantilly worth a day trip from Paris
how to get to Chantilly from Paris
is the Château de Vincennes worth visiting
what to see at Rambouillet
meta_title: Paris day trips by train: Chantilly, Rambouillet, Vincennes
meta_description: Three châteaux near Paris without the Versailles crowds: how to reach each by train or metro, what you see, and what each ticket includes.

featured_image.alt: The Château de Chantilly with its towers and slate roofs reflected in the water of its moat under a blue sky

content_html:
[place attraction="chateau-de-chantilly" city="paris"]

In April 1671 Louis XIV came to Chantilly with his court, as the guest of his cousin the Prince de Condé. The man in charge of feeding several thousand people for three days was the prince's steward, François Vatel. On the first evening the roast ran short at a few tables. The fireworks were spoiled by cloud. Vatel did not sleep.

The next day was a Friday, a day for fish, and he had ordered it from the Channel ports. At dawn only two loads had come. Vatel decided that no more was on the way, went up to his room, and killed himself with his sword. The rest of the fish arrived as he was found. Madame de Sévigné told the story in a letter, and Chantilly has told it ever since. The estate is 25 minutes from Paris by train. Two more are as easy to reach, and none of the three has the queues of Versailles.

The three at a glance

  • Chantilly: a château on water, a great collection of paintings, large gardens, the grandest stables in France. A full day.
  • Rambouillet: a small château of kings and presidents in a wide free park, with a dairy built for Marie Antoinette. Half a day to a day.
  • The Château de Vincennes: a medieval royal fortress at the edge of Paris, reached by metro. Two hours.

Chantilly

Regional trains from the Gare du Nord reach Chantilly-Gouvieux in about 25 minutes. The suburban line RER D goes there too, more slowly. From the station it is 20 to 25 minutes on foot, along the edge of the racecourse, or a short ride on a local bus.

The château is two buildings joined. The Petit Château dates from about 1560. The large one was destroyed after the Revolution and rebuilt between 1875 and 1882 for Henri d'Orléans, Duke of Aumale, a son of the last French king. He filled it with pictures and books and left the whole estate to the Institut de France, on condition that nothing be lent and that the hanging never change. So the Musée Condé still shows its paintings as he placed them, frame against frame: Raphael, Poussin, Ingres, and one of the best collections of old paintings in France outside the Louvre.

The gardens come in three parts: the formal parterres and canals laid out by André Le Nôtre, an Anglo-Chinese garden with a rustic hamlet of 1774 that gave Marie Antoinette the idea for hers at Versailles, and a later English garden. Across the lawn stand the Great Stables, built from 1719 for a prince who is said to have believed he would return as a horse. They hold a museum of the horse and a riding arena with shows.

The Grand Canal seen from the parterres laid out by André Le Nôtre at Chantilly. Photo: P.poschadel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.0 FR.

Rambouillet

Trains from the Gare Montparnasse take from 35 minutes to about an hour, depending on the stops. The château is ten to fifteen minutes on foot from the station, through the town.

It grew out of a medieval castle, of which one round tower is left. Francis I died in it in 1547. Louis XVI bought the estate in 1783 for the hunting, and Marie Antoinette is said to have disliked the place on sight. To win her round he had the Queen's Dairy built in the park, a small stone temple for tasting milk. Near it is the Shell Cottage, a thatched hut with a room lined in shells and mother-of-pearl. Napoleon had a small apartment fitted out, and Charles X signed his abdication here in 1830. For more than a century, until 2009, the château was a country residence of the presidents of the Republic, and the first summit of the large industrial countries met in it in 1975.

The rooms take about an hour. The park, with its canals and islands, is free and takes the rest of the afternoon. The dairy and the cottage are a walk into the park and open at set times.

The Château de Rambouillet from its garden. Photo: Trougnouf (Benoit Brummer), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Queen's Dairy, built in the park for Marie Antoinette in the 1780s. Photo: Chatsam, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The Château de Vincennes

Take metro line 1 to its eastern end, the station Château de Vincennes: about 20 minutes from the centre.

This was a main residence of the kings of France before Versailles. The keep, finished around 1370 under Charles V, is some 50 metres high, among the tallest medieval keeps in Europe. Henry V of England died at Vincennes in 1422. The chapel, begun in 1379 on the model of the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris, was finished only in the 1550s. Later the keep was a state prison: Diderot, Mirabeau and the Marquis de Sade were held in it, and the Duke of Enghien was shot in the moat in 1804.

Walking into the great courtyard is free. The ticket is for the keep and the chapel.

The fourteenth-century keep of the Château de Vincennes, seen from outside the castle. Photo: DXR, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

What each ticket includes

  • Château de Chantilly, gardens entry only: the three gardens and nothing else. The listing excludes the château with its paintings, the Great Stables and the horse show. If you want the pictures, you need the estate's own ticket instead, so decide before you buy.
  • Château de Rambouillet, entry ticket: the château and the emperor's apartment. The listing says there are no visits between 12:00 and 13:30, and that phone coverage is poor: download the ticket first. It does not name the dairy or the cottage, so ask at the desk.
  • Château de Vincennes ticket: entry to the keep and the chapel. The listing notes that the chapel closes for an hour at midday.
  • Château de Vincennes ticket and audio tour: the same entry with a commentary on your own phone that leads you through the castle. Bring earphones.
  • Villa Savoye, entry ticket: not a château. It is the white house on stilts that Le Corbusier built at Poissy between 1928 and 1931, a landmark of modern architecture. Poissy is on the RER A, and the house is a bus ride or a 20-minute walk uphill from the station.

These are the tickets our partner sells for these places, with today's prices:

[partner city="paris" match="chantilly,rambouillet,vincennes,savoye" limit="5"]

Which one

  • You have a whole day and like paintings or gardens: Chantilly.
  • You want quiet, a walk and a picnic: Rambouillet.
  • You have a free morning, or children who want a real castle: Vincennes.
  • It is raining: Vincennes, or Chantilly for the museum.

Each of these monuments has been closed one day a week, and the day is not the same everywhere. Check before you go: current hours are on our pages for the Château de Chantilly, the Château de Rambouillet and the Château de Vincennes.

From here

At Vincennes, the wood behind the castle holds a flower park, lakes and the Paris zoo. At Rambouillet, the national sheepfold founded by Louis XVI for his merino flock is at the far side of the park. For other days out, open the trip planner for France.

Cover photo: Basile Morin, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: How do you get to Chantilly from Paris?
faqs.a: By regional train from the Gare du Nord to Chantilly-Gouvieux, in about 25 minutes, or more slowly by RER D. The château is 20 to 25 minutes on foot from the station, or a short bus ride.

faqs.q: Is Chantilly worth a day trip from Paris?
faqs.a: Yes. It has a château on water, the paintings of the Musée Condé, gardens by Le Nôtre and the Great Stables, with far fewer visitors than Versailles.

faqs.q: Does the Chantilly gardens ticket include the château?
faqs.a: No. A gardens-only ticket covers the park. The château with its paintings, the Great Stables and the horse show are excluded.

faqs.q: Is the Château de Vincennes worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want a medieval castle without leaving Paris. It is at the end of metro line 1, the courtyard is free, and the ticket covers the keep and the chapel. Allow two hours.

faqs.q: What is there to see at Rambouillet?
faqs.a: The château, with the apartment of Napoleon, and a large free park with canals. In the park are the Queen's Dairy, built for Marie Antoinette, and the Shell Cottage.

title: A music walk in London: Soho, Denmark Street, Abbey Road and Camden, what is free and what has a ticket
subtitle: Almost everything on the rock map of London is a doorway, a plaque or a pedestrian crossing. One house has a ticket.
excerpt: Denmark Street, the clubs of Soho, the roof in Savile Row, the crossing at Abbey Road and the venues of Camden are all free to stand in front of. The Handel Hendrix House in Brook Street is the one place with a ticket. A route for one day, and what the audio tours and tickets include.
secondary_keywords: Abbey Road crossing how to get there
longtail_phrases: which tube station for the Abbey Road crossing
can you go inside Abbey Road Studios
is the Handel Hendrix House worth visiting
where did the Beatles play their last concert in London
rock and roll sites in Soho
meta_title: London music walk: Soho, Abbey Road, Camden
meta_description: Denmark Street, Soho, Savile Row, Abbey Road and Camden in one day: what is free to stand in front of, and the one house that needs a ticket.

featured_image.alt: The black and white stripes of the pedestrian crossing on Abbey Road in London, with trees and a red brick mansion block behind

content_html:
[place attraction="handel-hendrix-house" city="london"]

In 1968 Jimi Hendrix took a small flat at the top of 23 Brook Street, in Mayfair, with his girlfriend Kathy Etchingham, who had found it through a newspaper advertisement. They bought curtains and cushions at the John Lewis shop round the corner, and he called it the first real home of his own.

On the wall of the house next door was a blue plaque: George Frideric Handel had lived at number 25 from 1723 until his death in 1759, and had written Messiah in it. Hendrix, the story goes, went out and bought records of Handel's music. Two musicians, two centuries apart, on the two sides of one wall: London's music history is like that, close together and mostly hidden behind ordinary front doors. Nearly all of it is free to look at from the pavement. This is a route through it for one day, with the one place where you pay to go in.

What is free and what has a ticket

  • Free, from the street: Denmark Street, the Soho addresses, 3 Savile Row, the plaques in Brook Street, the Abbey Road crossing and the outside of the studios, the Camden venues and markets.
  • Ticket: the Handel Hendrix House.
  • A ticket of another kind: the clubs that are still clubs. Ronnie Scott's, the 100 Club, the Roundhouse, Koko and the Electric Ballroom open for concerts, and you get in by buying one.

Denmark Street and Soho

Start at Tottenham Court Road station. Denmark Street, a hundred metres long, was London's Tin Pan Alley: music publishers from the early 1900s, then studios and instrument shops. The Rolling Stones recorded their first album at Regent Sounds, at number 4, in 1964. The Sex Pistols lived and rehearsed in an outbuilding behind number 6 in the mid-1970s. The guitar shops are still there, though the block around the street has been rebuilt in recent years.

From there Soho is a ten-minute wander:

  • 100 Oxford Street: the 100 Club, a basement that has had live music since the 1940s and held the punk festival of 1976.
  • 90 Wardour Street: the site of the Marquee Club from 1964 to 1988, where the Who, Hendrix and David Bowie played. A plaque marks it.
  • St Anne's Court: the alley of Trident Studios, where the Beatles recorded Hey Jude and Bowie made his early albums.
  • 59 Old Compton Street: the 2i's Coffee Bar, where British rock and roll began in the late 1950s. Another plaque.
  • 47 Frith Street: Ronnie Scott's, the jazz club, here since 1965. Hendrix played in public for the last time on its stage, in September 1970.
  • Heddon Street, off Regent Street: where Bowie was photographed for the cover of Ziggy Stardust in 1972.

Denmark Street in 2013, looking west. The guitar shops are on both sides. Photo: morebyless, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

Savile Row and Brook Street

At 3 Savile Row, the headquarters of the Beatles' company Apple, the group played on the roof at lunchtime on 30 January 1969. It was their last performance in public, and the police came up to stop it. The building is private. You look at the front and the plaque.

Ten minutes north is Brook Street. The Handel Hendrix House joins numbers 23 and 25. In Handel's house you see the rooms where he lived, composed and rehearsed for thirty-six years, furnished as a Georgian house and often with a harpsichord being played. Up the stairs next door is the Hendrix flat: one main room, put back as it was in 1969 from photographs and from Kathy Etchingham's memory, and a room about his time in London. The museum reopened in 2023 after a long restoration. Allow an hour to an hour and a half, and expect stairs.

Brook Street: the plaque for Hendrix on the white house at number 23, the one for Handel on number 25. Photo: Oosoom, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The room of Jimi Hendrix on the top floor of 23 Brook Street, furnished again as it was in 1969. Photo: AndyScott, via Wikimedia Commons, CC0.

Abbey Road

From Bond Street station, a few minutes from Brook Street, the Jubilee line takes you two stops north to St John's Wood. The crossing is five minutes on foot from there. Do not go to the station called Abbey Road: it is on the Docklands Light Railway in east London, on the other side of the city, and it catches visitors all the time.

The photograph for the album cover was taken on the morning of 8 August 1969, in about ten minutes, while a policeman held the traffic. The crossing has been a listed monument since 2010. It is also a working road with buses on it, so be quick and watch the cars. The studios at number 3, opened in 1931, are not open to visitors. There is a shop beside them, and the low wall in front is covered in messages that are painted over regularly.

Round the corner at 7 Cavendish Avenue is the house Paul McCartney bought in the 1960s. It is still a private home.

Camden

From St John's Wood it is about half an hour on foot to Camden along the north side of Regent's Park, or a short bus or taxi ride. The Roundhouse, at Chalk Farm, is a railway engine shed of 1847 that became a concert hall in the 1960s: Pink Floyd and the Doors played in it, and the Ramones in July 1976. Down the high street are the Electric Ballroom, the markets around Camden Lock, the bronze statue of Amy Winehouse in the Stables Market, and at the far end Koko, a theatre of 1900 that has been a music venue under several names.

Camden Lock on the Regent's Canal, the middle of the market. Photo: Oxyman, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.5.

What the audio tours and tickets include

  • Handel Hendrix House, entry ticket: admission to both houses, with an audio guide online. The only listing here that takes you inside a place on this route.
  • Rock'n'roll Legacy audio tour: a self-guided walk on your phone, two and a half hours. Its listing gives a start in New Oxford Street and an end in Wimpole Street, yet names Abbey Road among the highlights: read the route before you buy.
  • Rock 'n' Roll Beginnings audio tour: starts at Abbey Road and ends in Denmark Street, about eight kilometres, on the Beatles and the Rolling Stones. Transport between the two ends is at your cost.
  • Camden Musical audio tour: an hour and a half around Camden Lock and the high street.
  • Hard Rock Cafe London Piccadilly, skip the line: not a museum ticket. It is a table without queueing and a burger at the branch on Piccadilly Circus, among cases of guitars and stage clothes.

None of the audio tours includes entry to anything, and you need your own earphones. These are the products our partner sells for this route, with today's prices:

[partner city="london" match="rock,roll,camden,musical,hendrix,handel" limit="5"]

From here

Stay in Camden for the evening: this is where the day's history is still going on, in pubs with a stage at the back. Current hours for the museum are on our page for the Handel Hendrix House. See what else there is in London, or open the trip planner for the United Kingdom.

Cover photo: Misterweiss, via Wikimedia Commons.

faqs.q: Which tube station is nearest to the Abbey Road crossing?
faqs.a: St John's Wood, on the Jubilee line, five minutes on foot from the crossing. The station called Abbey Road is in east London and is the wrong one.

faqs.q: Can you go inside Abbey Road Studios?
faqs.a: No. They are working recording studios and are not open to visitors. You can see the building from the street, use the crossing and visit the shop next door.

faqs.q: Is the Handel Hendrix House worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if you care about either musician. You see the Georgian rooms where Handel lived for thirty-six years and the flat of Jimi Hendrix, put back as it was in 1969. Allow an hour to an hour and a half.

faqs.q: Where did the Beatles play their last concert?
faqs.a: On the roof of 3 Savile Row in London, the office of their company Apple, on 30 January 1969. The building is private and is seen from the street.

faqs.q: Is a music walk in London free?
faqs.a: Almost entirely. Denmark Street, the Soho addresses, Savile Row, Abbey Road and Camden cost nothing to see from outside. The Handel Hendrix House has a ticket, and the clubs charge for concerts.

title: Rembrandt in Amsterdam: the Rembrandt House, the Night Watch or an "experience", and which to pay for
subtitle: His house has his etchings and no great paintings. His paintings hang across town. Two shows have neither. Which is which.
excerpt: The Rembrandt House is where he lived and worked. The Night Watch hangs in the Rijksmuseum. Two "experience" attractions show projections and no originals. What each one really is, what is free to see on foot, and which ticket to buy.
longtail_phrases: is the Rembrandt House Museum worth it
are there Rembrandt paintings in the Rembrandt House
where can I see the Night Watch in Amsterdam
what is the Rembrandts Amsterdam Experience
where did Rembrandt live in Amsterdam
meta_title: Rembrandt in Amsterdam: house, Night Watch or experience
meta_description: The Rembrandt House, the Night Watch in the Rijksmuseum and two projection shows: what each really is, what is free, and which ticket to buy.

featured_image.alt: Visitors in the Gallery of Honour of the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam, with the Night Watch on the end wall under a painted vault

content_html:
[place attraction="rembrandt-house-museum" city="amsterdam"]

In July 1656 officials of the insolvency chamber of Amsterdam went through a house in the Sint Antoniesbreestraat room by room and wrote down everything in it. The owner, Rembrandt van Rijn, could not pay his debts. He had bought the house in 1639, at the height of his success, for thirteen thousand guilders to be paid in instalments, and he had never finished paying.

They listed the paintings on every wall, the beds, the chairs, the busts of Roman emperors, the shells and corals, the weapons, the albums of prints by other artists that he had collected for years. Everything was sold. He moved to a rented house on the Rozengracht and died there in 1669. That inventory survives, and it is the reason his house could be furnished again three centuries later. It is also why "Rembrandt in Amsterdam" means several different visits, some with a ticket and some without, and they are easy to confuse.

Which is which

  • The Rembrandt House Museum: the real house, refurnished. His etchings, his studio, almost no paintings by him. Ticket.
  • The Rijksmuseum: the paintings. The Night Watch and a room of others. Ticket, with a start time.
  • Rembrandts Amsterdam Experience: a filmed and projected show about his life. No originals. Ticket.
  • Van Gogh and Rembrandt in Amsterdam: a sound and light show in a church. No originals. Ticket.
  • The streets: the places where he lived, worked and was buried. Free.

The Rembrandt House

The house stands at Jodenbreestraat 4, five minutes from the Nieuwmarkt. It was built in 1606, the year he was born. He lived in it from 1639 to 1658, and painted the Night Watch while he lived here. It has been a museum since 1911, and in the 1990s the rooms were put back to the seventeenth century with the inventory as a guide.

You go in through the modern building next door and climb through the old house floor by floor: the kitchen with its box bed, the entrance hall where he sold pictures, the room of curiosities, and at the top the large north-facing studio and the smaller one where his pupils worked. Through the middle of the day, staff show how an etching was printed and how paint was ground from pigment and oil.

What the museum owns is his graphic work: nearly all of the roughly three hundred etchings he made, shown a selection at a time. The paintings on the walls are by his teacher, his pupils and his contemporaries. If you came for famous canvases, this is the wrong address. If you want to understand how he worked, it is the right one. Allow an hour to an hour and a half. The old house has steep stairs and no lift.

The house Rembrandt bought in 1639. The entrance is through the modern building on the left. Photo: Hide-sp, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

The etching press in the Rembrandt House, where printing is demonstrated. Photo: Steven Lek, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The Night Watch, in the Rijksmuseum

The Night Watch was finished in 1642 for the hall of a company of civic guards. It shows the company of Captain Frans Banninck Cocq setting out, and it is not a night scene: the name came later, when the varnish had darkened. The canvas measures about 3.6 by 4.4 metres and was once larger. When it was moved to the town hall in 1715 it did not fit between two doors, and strips were cut from all four sides.

It hangs at the end of the Gallery of Honour, on the second floor of the Rijksmuseum. Since 2019 the museum has been studying and restoring it where it hangs, inside a glass room, so you may see conservators or equipment in front of it. Near it are his other great pictures: the Jewish Bride, the Syndics of the drapers' guild, a late self-portrait. Half an hour is enough for these alone, though nobody stops there.

The Night Watch, finished in 1642. The captain in black is Frans Banninck Cocq. Photo: Rijksmuseum, via Wikimedia Commons.

The two "experience" attractions

Rembrandts Amsterdam Experience is, by its listing, a show of about 25 minutes in a reconstruction of his last studio on the Rozengracht, with film and projection, in which you meet the painter and his household. You choose a language on arrival and may wait for the next showing in it.

Van Gogh and Rembrandt in Amsterdam is a sound and light show inside the Noorderkerk, a church of the 1620s in the Jordaan, with the works of the two painters projected large on its walls and readings from Van Gogh's letters. Its listing states that entry to the Van Gogh Museum and to the Rembrandt museum is not included.

Neither shows an original work. They are introductions, good with children or on a wet evening, and no substitute for the two museums.

What is free: Rembrandt on foot

  • The Waag, on the Nieuwmarkt: the surgeons' guild met upstairs, and for it he painted the Anatomy Lesson of Dr Tulp in 1632. The picture is now in The Hague.
  • The Zuiderkerk, behind the house: three of his children, who died as infants, were buried here.
  • The Nieuwe Doelenstraat: the site of the guards' hall for which the Night Watch was made. A hotel stands there now.
  • The Rembrandtplein: his statue of 1852, the oldest public statue in the city.
  • Rozengracht 184: a plaque on the site of the house where he died.
  • The Westerkerk: he was buried here in October 1669 in a rented grave. Nobody knows where it was. A memorial is on a pillar inside.

The Westerkerk, where Rembrandt was buried in 1669 in a grave that has not been found. Photo: Dietmar Rabich, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What each ticket includes

  • Rembrandt House Museum ticket and audio city walk: entry to the house, plus a walk of about three kilometres on your phone through the old Jewish quarter and along the Amstel. The partner's commentary is for the streets only. Inside, the museum has its own guide.
  • Rijksmuseum ticket and highlights audio tour with a city walk: entry to the museum, a commentary on its main works on your phone, and a walk afterwards through the east of the centre. It is entry to the whole museum, not only to Rembrandt.
  • Rembrandts Amsterdam Experience, entry ticket: the show. The listing notes there is no toilet on the premises.
  • Van Gogh and Rembrandt in Amsterdam, admission ticket: the show in the church. Check that it is running on your dates.

These are the tickets our partner sells for Rembrandt in Amsterdam, with today's prices:

[partner city="amsterdam" match="rembrandt,house,rijksmuseum" limit="4"]

Which to pay for

  • One ticket only: the Rijksmuseum. The paintings are the point.
  • Two: add the Rembrandt House, on another day or after a break. Together they are the painter and his work.
  • With children under ten, or an hour to fill in the Jordaan: one of the shows.

From here

From the Rembrandt House, the flea market on the Waterlooplein and the Portuguese Synagogue are a few minutes away. Current hours are on our page for the Rembrandt House Museum. See what else there is in Amsterdam, or open the trip planner for the Netherlands.

Cover photo: Hnapel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is the Rembrandt House Museum worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, if you want to see how he lived and worked: the house is refurnished from an inventory of 1656 and etching is demonstrated daily. It holds his etchings and almost none of his paintings.

faqs.q: Are there Rembrandt paintings in the Rembrandt House?
faqs.a: Hardly any. The museum owns nearly all of his etchings and shows them in turn. The paintings on its walls are mostly by his teacher, pupils and contemporaries.

faqs.q: Where can you see the Night Watch in Amsterdam?
faqs.a: In the Rijksmuseum, at the end of the Gallery of Honour on the second floor. It has been under study and restoration inside a glass room since 2019 and stays on view.

faqs.q: What is the Rembrandts Amsterdam Experience?
faqs.a: A show of about 25 minutes with film and projection about the painter's life, set in a reconstruction of his last studio. It shows no original works.

faqs.q: Where is Rembrandt buried?
faqs.a: In the Westerkerk in Amsterdam, where he was buried in a rented grave in October 1669. The exact place is unknown, and a memorial inside the church marks the fact.

title: Utrecht as a day trip from Amsterdam: the Dom tower, the wharf canals and the museum quarter, what is free and what needs a ticket
subtitle: Half an hour by train to a city whose cathedral lost its middle in a storm and whose canals have a second street at water level.
excerpt: Utrecht is under half an hour from Amsterdam by train. The canals with their wharves, the cathedral and its cloister are free. The Dom tower, the excavations under the square and the museums need a ticket. A route for one day, and what the audio walks include.

content_html:
[place attraction="st-martin-s-cathedral-utrecht" city="utrecht"]

On the evening of 1 August 1674 a storm crossed Utrecht in a quarter of an hour. It took the roofs off houses and the spires off churches, and it brought down the whole nave of the cathedral. The nave had been built last and cheaply, without the flying buttresses the plan called for, and it folded. The tower at one end and the choir at the other stayed up.

The city never rebuilt it. The rubble lay where it fell for a century and a half before it was cleared, and the gap became a square. That is why the tallest church tower in the Netherlands stands alone today, across the paving from its own church. It is the first thing to understand about Utrecht and it is free to look at. The city is under half an hour from Amsterdam, small enough to walk, and much of what makes it worth the trip costs nothing.

Getting there

Intercity trains run from Amsterdam Centraal to Utrecht Centraal several times an hour through the day and take a little under half an hour. You need no reservation. The station opens into the Hoog Catharijne shopping centre: walk through it, cross the rebuilt canal at its far side, and you are in the old town. The Dom tower is ten to fifteen minutes from the platform, and you can see it most of the way.

What is free and what needs a ticket

  • Free: the canals and their wharves, the Domplein, the cathedral (a donation is asked), the cloister garden, the courtyards and almshouses, the Letters of Utrecht.
  • Ticket: the climb of the Dom tower, the excavations under the square, every museum, the Rietveld Schröder House, a boat on the canal.

The Dom tower, the square and the cathedral

The tower was built between 1321 and 1382 and is about 112 metres high. You can go up only with a guide, at a booked time, by 465 steps: there is no lift. The way up passes two chapels and the bells before the gallery at the top, from which Amsterdam is visible on a clear day. A long restoration ended in 2024. Tours sell out at weekends, so book ahead.

On the square, lines in the paving mark where the lost nave stood. Beneath it, a ticketed visit called DOMunder takes you down with a torch among the foundations of the Roman fort from which the city grew, and the debris of 1674.

What is left of the cathedral, the choir and the transept, is open and free. Beside it, through a gate, is the Pandhof: a Gothic cloister around a garden of herbs, one of the quietest places in the centre.

The Dom tower closes the view from many streets of the old centre. Photo: Myxomato, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

The Pandhof, the cloister garden of the cathedral. It is free to walk into. Photo: Gerd Eichmann, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The canals with a lower street

The Oudegracht runs through the whole old town, and it is unlike the canals of Amsterdam. The water lies well below the street. Along it, at water level, is a second quay, the wharf, and behind the wharf deep cellars run back under the roadway to the houses. Merchants in the Middle Ages unloaded straight from the boat into the cellar. Today the cellars are restaurants, workshops and bars, and the wharves are terraces where you sit level with the passing boats.

Walk the Oudegracht from north to south, going down the steps and up again as you like. Then return by the Nieuwegracht, one street to the east, which has the same wharves, more trees and almost nobody on it. Along the Oudegracht look for the Letters of Utrecht: a poem carved into the kerb stones, one letter added every Saturday since 2012, meant to go on for as long as someone pays for the next stone.

A wharf on the Oudegracht: the cellar doors are at water level, the street is above the wall. Photo: Ymblanter, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The museum quarter

The southern end of the old town is called the museum quarter. All of these have their own ticket:

  • The Centraal Museum: the city's museum, founded in 1838. Utrecht painters of the seventeenth century, a ship a thousand years old, and furniture by Gerrit Rietveld.
  • The Miffy museum across the street, for small children. Dick Bruna, who drew the rabbit, lived and worked in Utrecht.
  • Museum Catharijneconvent: religious art of the Netherlands in a former convent.
  • The Railway Museum, in a station of 1874 east of the centre: the best choice with children.
  • Museum Speelklok, in a medieval church near the Dom: musical clocks, music boxes and street organs that play by themselves. Go round with a guide, who sets the instruments going.
  • The Rietveld Schröder House of 1924, at the eastern edge of town: a house of sliding walls and primary colours, on the World Heritage list. Visits are by reservation only.

One museum and the tower are enough for a day. With more, you stop seeing the city.

The Rietveld Schröder House of 1924, at the eastern edge of the city. Photo: Husky, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

What our partner sells for Utrecht: audio walks

To be plain: the block below shows audio walks, not tickets. Our partner does not sell the Dom tower or the Utrecht museums in its Utrecht list. Each walk is a route with commentary that you download to your phone. None includes entry to anything, and you need earphones.

  • City Centre's Pulse: the longest, about an hour and a half and four kilometres, from the station hall to the Domplein by way of the southern canals and the cloister.
  • Faith, Art, and Stone: a short walk of about forty minutes from the Mariaplaats to the Domplein.
  • Museum Quarter Historical: about an hour, also from the Mariaplaats to the Domplein. Its route overlaps the one above, so take one of the two.
  • Echoes of History: about an hour through the northern half of the centre, which the others leave out.

The partner does sell entry to Museum Speelklok, filed under Amsterdam: you find it on our page for the museum, linked above. These are the audio walks, with today's prices:

[partner city="utrecht" match="utrecht" limit="4"]

A day in order

  • Morning: train, the walk in, the Domplein, the cathedral and the cloister. The tower, if you booked it.
  • Midday: lunch on a wharf of the Oudegracht.
  • Afternoon: south along the canal to the museum quarter, one museum, and back by the Nieuwegracht.

From here

Trains back to Amsterdam run until late, so there is no need to hurry dinner. If you have a second day in the region, Castle De Haar is a short trip west of the city. See what else there is in Utrecht, or open the trip planner for the Netherlands.

faqs.q: Is Utrecht worth a day trip from Amsterdam?
faqs.a: Yes. It is under half an hour away by train, compact enough to walk, and has canals with wharves at water level, the tallest church tower in the Netherlands and a good group of museums.

faqs.q: How long is the train from Amsterdam to Utrecht?
faqs.a: A little under half an hour by intercity from Amsterdam Centraal to Utrecht Centraal. Trains run several times an hour during the day and need no reservation.

faqs.q: Can you climb the Dom tower in Utrecht?
faqs.a: Yes, with a guide and at a booked time. There are 465 steps and no lift, and tours often sell out at weekends.

faqs.q: What is free to see in Utrecht?
faqs.a: The canals and their wharves, the Domplein, the cathedral, the Pandhof cloister garden, the old courtyards and the Letters of Utrecht. The tower, the excavations under the square and the museums need a ticket.

faqs.q: Why is the Dom tower separate from the church?
faqs.a: Because the nave that joined them collapsed in a storm on 1 August 1674 and was never rebuilt. The square between the tower and the choir is where it stood.
